learn.hook: A Diwali sale banner says '25% OFF'. That is just a fraction wearing a disguise: 25/100, which is one quarter off!
points: Per cent means 'per hundred'. 35% = 35/100 = 0.35.
To change a fraction to a percentage, multiply by 100: 3/4 = 3/4 × 100% = 75%, and 1/8 = 12.5%.
x% of a quantity = quantity × x/100. So 20% of ₹450 = ₹450 × 20/100 = ₹90.
What percentage is a of b? Work out a/b × 100. Getting 18 out of 24 is 18/24 × 100 = 75%.
Finding the whole: if 30% of a number is 45, the number is 45 × 100/30 = 150.

example.q: Kabir scored 42 out of 60 in a quiz. What percentage did he score?

learn.reallife: Marks in exams, battery levels on a phone, the chance of rain and interest in a bank are all shown as percentages.

quiz.q: What is 35% as a fraction in simplest form?
quiz.explain: 35% = 35/100. Divide top and bottom by 5 to get 7/20.
quiz.mistake: Simplifies wrongly or forgets that per cent means out of 100

quiz.q: Riya scored 42 out of 60 in a test. What percentage did she score?
quiz.mistake: Writes the marks scored as the percentage without dividing by the total

quiz.q: What is 20% of ₹450?
quiz.mistake: Finds 10% instead of 20%, or subtracts 20 from 450

quiz.q: Write 3/8 as a percentage.
quiz.mistake: Writes the decimal 0.375 with a % sign without multiplying by 100

quiz.q: In a school, 30% of the students come by bus. If 45 students come by bus, how many students are there in the school?
quiz.explain: 30% of the total is 45, so 1% is 45 ÷ 30 = 1.5 and 100% is 150.
quiz.mistake: Finds 30% of 45 (13.5) instead of the whole

quiz.q: Which of these has the largest value: 5/8, 0.6, 61%, 0.59?
quiz.explain: Turn all into decimals: 5/8 = 0.625, 0.6, 61% = 0.61, 0.59. So 5/8 is the largest.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 61% is largest because 61 is a big number

quiz.q: A cricket team won 18 out of 24 matches and lost the rest. What percentage of matches did it lose?
quiz.mistake: Gives the winning percentage (75%) instead of the losing percentage

quiz.q: Meena spends 40% of her ₹500 pocket money on books. How much money is left?
quiz.mistake: Gives the amount spent instead of the amount left

teach.ask: Gappu asks: What does 25% really mean? Is it 25 rupees?
teach.praise: 25% means 25 out of every 100, which is the fraction 25/100 = 1/4. Not always 25 rupees! Thanks!
teach.nudge: What does 'per cent' mean? Can you write 25% as a fraction?

topics.title: Percentages around us and in your head

learn.hook: Your body is about 60% water, a chips packet may be 35% fat, and 10% of anything is just one easy division away!
points: Percentages are everywhere: food labels (sugar 20% of the packet), the body (about 60% water) and surveys (45% of students prefer cricket).
Building blocks for mental maths: 10% = divide by 10; 5% = half of 10%; 20% = double 10%; 25% = one quarter; 1% = divide by 100.
Estimating a/b as a percent: 7/9 is a bit less than 8/10, about 78%; 5/7 is about 71%.
Bar model: draw a bar for 100% and split it into 10 equal parts of 10% each. Shade the parts you need.
learn.reallife: At a sale, '25% off on ₹1,200' is ₹300 off — a quarter — and you can work it out before reaching the counter.

quiz.q: What is 15% of ₹360?
quiz.mistake: Finds only 10%

quiz.q: What is 35% of 240?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the extra 5%

quiz.q: What is 5% of ₹1280?
quiz.explain: 10% is ₹128, so 5% is half of that: ₹64.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 10%

quiz.q: About what percentage is 7/9?
quiz.mistake: Treats 7/9 as 70% by looking at the 7 only

quiz.q: A bar for a 240 km trip is split into 10 equal parts. 3 parts are shaded. How many km is that?
quiz.explain: Each part is 10% = 24 km, so 3 parts = 30% = 72 km.
quiz.mistake: Reads the 3 parts as 30 km

quiz.q: About 60% of the human body is water. About how much water is in a 45 kg child?
quiz.mistake: Uses the 60 as kilograms

quiz.q: A 30 g snack packet label says sugar is 20% of the weight. How much sugar is in it?
quiz.mistake: Reads the percentage as grams

quiz.q: In a survey of 600 students, 45% prefer cricket. How many students is that?
quiz.mistake: Takes 45 as the number of students

teach.ask: Gappu needs 25% of 840 seeds for his garden but has no calculator. How can he work it out in his head?
teach.praise: 25% is a quarter: 840 ÷ 4 = 210. Halve, then halve again — easy!
teach.nudge: Which simple fraction is the same as 25%?

learn.hook: Your height grew from 140 cm to 147 cm and your little cousin's from 70 cm to 77 cm. Both grew 7 cm, but who grew more in percentage?
points: Percentage change = (change ÷ original value) × 100.
Always divide by the ORIGINAL (starting) value, not the new value.
Increase by r%: new value = original × (100 + r)/100. So ₹200 up by 10% = ₹200 × 1.1 = ₹220.
Decrease by r%: new value = original × (100 − r)/100. So ₹500 down by 20% = ₹500 × 0.8 = ₹400.
Up 10% then down 10% does NOT bring you back: 100 → 110 → 99.

example.q: A cricket bat's price rose from ₹800 to ₹1000. Find the percentage increase.

learn.reallife: News reports say things like 'petrol price up 5%' or 'school enrolment up 12%'. Percent change lets us compare fairly.

items.text: Going from 40 to 50 is a ___ increase
Going from 50 to 40 is a ___ decrease

games.title: Percent puzzles
items: Going from 40 to 50 and going from 50 to 40 are the same percentage change.
Increasing by 10% and then decreasing by 10% brings you back to the start.
A 100% increase means the amount doubles.
Adding 100% of the amount adds the whole amount again.
To increase a number by 25%, you can multiply it by 1.25.
Percentage change is found by dividing the change by the new value.
We always divide by the original value.

quiz.q: The price of a cricket bat rose from ₹800 to ₹1000. What is the percentage increase?
quiz.mistake: Divides by the new price (200/1000 = 20%)

quiz.q: A village has 5000 people. The population grows by 8%. What is the new population?
quiz.mistake: Adds 8 instead of 8%

quiz.q: A school bag costs ₹1200. Its price is reduced by 15%. What is the new price?
quiz.mistake: Gives only the reduction (₹180) or adds it

quiz.q: Aisha's marks went down from 60 to 45. What is the percentage decrease?
quiz.mistake: Divides by the new value 45 (gets 33 1/3%)

quiz.q: Start with 100. Increase it by 10%, then decrease the result by 10%. What is the final number?
quiz.explain: 100 + 10% = 110. Then 10% of 110 is 11, and 110 − 11 = 99. The second 10% is of a bigger number.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two 10% changes cancel out

quiz.q: A train ticket costs ₹400 after a 25% increase. What was the original price?
quiz.explain: New price = 125% of original. So original = 400 × 100/125 = ₹320. Check: 25% of 320 = 80, and 320 + 80 = 400.
quiz.mistake: Takes 25% off ₹400 (gets ₹300), but the 25% was of the original price

quiz.q: A shop sold 250 boxes of diyas last Diwali and 400 boxes this Diwali. What is the percentage increase?
quiz.mistake: Divides by the new value 400 (37.5%) or gives the increase itself

quiz.q: To decrease a price by 30%, you can multiply it by which number?
quiz.explain: After a 30% decrease, 70% of the price is left. 70% = 0.7.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 0.3, which gives the decrease instead of the new price

teach.ask: Gappu asks: Something went from 40 to 50. How do I find the percentage increase?
teach.praise: The change is 10, divide by the original 40, and multiply by 100: 25%. Perfect!
teach.nudge: First find how much it changed. Then which number do you divide by: 40 or 50?

learn.hook: A shopkeeper marks a kurta at ₹800, gives a 20% discount, and still makes a profit. How? It cost him only ₹500!
points: Cost price (CP) is what the seller paid. Selling price (SP) is what the buyer pays.
If SP > CP there is a profit: Profit = SP − CP. If CP > SP there is a loss: Loss = CP − SP.
Profit % and loss % are always worked out on the cost price: Profit % = Profit/CP × 100.
Marked price (MP) is the price on the tag. Discount = MP − SP, and discount % is worked out on the marked price.
After a discount of r%, SP = MP × (100 − r)/100.

example.q: A kurta costs the shopkeeper ₹500. He marks it at ₹800 and gives a 20% discount. Find the SP and the profit percentage.

learn.reallife: Festival sales, sabzi mandi bargains and school fete stalls all involve cost price, selling price and discounts.

quiz.q: Arjun buys a cycle for ₹3000 and sells it for ₹3600. What is his profit percentage?
quiz.mistake: Divides the profit by the selling price (gets 16 2/3%)

quiz.q: Meena buys a lamp for ₹450 and sells it for ₹360. What is her loss percentage?
quiz.mistake: Divides the loss by the selling price (gets 25%)

quiz.q: A saree marked at ₹2500 is sold at a 12% discount. What is the selling price?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts ₹12 instead of 12%, or gives only the discount

quiz.q: A shirt marked at ₹800 is sold for ₹680. What is the discount percentage?
quiz.mistake: Gives the discount in rupees as a percentage, or gives the percentage paid (85%)

quiz.q: A shopkeeper buys a toy for ₹200 and wants a profit of 25%. At what price should he sell it?
quiz.mistake: Adds ₹25 instead of 25%, or gives only the profit

quiz.q: On which price is the profit percentage calculated?
quiz.explain: Profit and loss percentages are always found on the cost price, the price the seller paid.
quiz.mistake: Uses the selling price as the base

quiz.q: A fruit seller buys 12 mangoes for ₹240 and sells them at ₹25 each. What is his total profit?
quiz.mistake: Gives the profit on one mango (₹5) instead of all 12

quiz.q: Kabir marks a bag at ₹1000 and gives a 20% discount. The bag cost him ₹640. What is his profit percentage?
quiz.mistake: Divides the profit by the marked price (gets 16%)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: I bought a toy for ₹100 and sold it for ₹120. How do I find my profit percentage?
teach.praise: Profit = ₹120 − ₹100 = ₹20, and 20 out of the cost ₹100 is 20%. I am a smart shopkeeper now!
teach.nudge: How much extra did you get? And which price do you compare it with?

learn.hook: A shop raises a price by 20% and then gives '20% off'. Do you pay the old price? No — you pay less, and the shop loses!
points: Percentages can be more than 100: 150% of 80 = 1.5 × 80 = 120. If a price becomes 2.5 times, the new price is 250% of the old (a 150% increase).
GST is added as a percentage of the price: ₹800 + 18% GST = 800 × 1.18 = ₹944.
Marking up by r% and then giving r% off ends below the start: 100 → 120 → 96 for r = 20. That is a 4% loss.
Area changes multiply: if each side of a square grows by 10%, the area becomes 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21 times — a 21% increase, not 20%.
If length goes up 20% and breadth goes down 20%, the area becomes 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 times — a 4% decrease.

example.q: A shopkeeper buys a fan for ₹500, marks it up by 20%, and then gives 20% off. Profit or loss?

learn.reallife: Bills at restaurants and shops in India show GST separately — now you can check it yourself.

games.title: Tricky or true?
items: Marking up by 25% and then giving 25% off gets back the cost price.
If each side of a square doubles, its area becomes 4 times.
300% of a number is 3 times the number.

quiz.q: What is 150% of 80?
quiz.mistake: Thinks a percentage cannot be more than 100

quiz.q: What is 250% of 60?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2.5 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: A school bag costs ₹800 before GST. With 18% GST, what is the final price?
quiz.mistake: Adds ₹18 instead of 18%

quiz.q: A restaurant bill is ₹1200 before tax. With 5% GST, what is the total?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the tax

quiz.q: A shopkeeper buys a toy for ₹500, marks it up by 20%, then gives a 20% discount. How much money does he lose?
quiz.explain: Marked price ₹600; after 20% off, SP = ₹480. Loss = 500 − 480 = ₹20.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal percentages cancel out

quiz.q: A price is marked up by 25% and then reduced by 25%. What is the overall percentage loss?
quiz.explain: 1.25 × 0.75 = 0.9375, which is 93.75% of the original — a 6.25% loss.
quiz.mistake: Assumes +25% and −25% cancel

quiz.q: Each side of a square increases by 10%. By what percentage does its area increase?
quiz.explain: New area = 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21 times the old, a 21% increase.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the percentage instead of multiplying the factors

quiz.q: A rectangle's length is increased by 20% and its breadth is decreased by 20%. By what percentage does its area decrease?
quiz.explain: New area = 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 times the old, so it decreases by 4%.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two changes cancel

teach.ask: Gappu's shop marked a toy up by 10% and then gave 10% off. He thinks he is back where he started. Is he?
teach.praise: Oh no! 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99, so I lost 1%. Percentages of different wholes don't cancel!
teach.nudge: Is 10% of the new price the same as 10% of the old price?

learn.hook: Put ₹1000 in a bank at 10% and leave it. With compound interest it is ₹1210 after 2 years — interest earns interest!
points: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount p: amount after t years = p(1 + rt). ₹5000 at 8% for 3 years: 5000 × 1.24 = ₹6200.
Compound interest adds each year's interest to the amount, so next year's interest is bigger: amount = p(1 + r)ᵗ. ₹5000 at 8% for 3 years: 5000 × 1.08³ ≈ ₹6298.56.
Depreciation (losing value) works by repeated multiplication too: a scooter worth ₹60,000 losing 10% a year is worth 60,000 × 0.9 × 0.9 = ₹48,600 after 2 years.
Populations and prices (inflation) grow the same way: 20,000 people growing 5% a year become 20,000 × 1.05² = 22,050 after 2 years.
Percentage share: a family spending ₹12,000 of ₹40,000 on food spends 30% on food.

example.q: Compare simple and compound interest on ₹1000 at 10% for 2 years.
steps: Compound gives ₹10 more (interest on the first year's interest)

learn.reallife: Bank fixed deposits, home loans and even the value of a used phone all follow these rules.

quiz.q: ₹2000 is deposited at 5% simple interest per year. What is the amount after 4 years?
quiz.mistake: Uses compound growth or forgets to add the principal

quiz.q: ₹1000 is deposited at 10% compound interest per year. What is the amount after 2 years?
quiz.mistake: Uses simple interest

quiz.q: For ₹1000 at 10% for 2 years, how much more does compound interest give than simple interest?
quiz.explain: Compound gives ₹1210, simple gives ₹1200. The extra ₹10 is 10% of the first year's ₹100 interest.
quiz.mistake: Thinks both kinds of interest are equal

quiz.q: A scooter worth ₹60,000 loses 10% of its value every year. What is it worth after 2 years?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 10% of the original price both years

quiz.q: A phone costing ₹20,000 depreciates by 20% each year. What is its value after 2 years?
quiz.mistake: Takes 40% off at once

quiz.q: A town of 20,000 people grows by 5% each year. What is its population after 2 years?
quiz.mistake: Adds 5% of the original each year

quiz.q: With 6% inflation, a ₹50 notebook will cost how much next year?
quiz.mistake: Adds 6 rupees instead of 6%

quiz.q: A family earns ₹40,000 a month and spends ₹12,000 on food. What percentage is spent on food?
quiz.mistake: Divides the wrong way round

teach.ask: Gappu's grandpa says compound interest is 'interest on interest'. What does that mean?
teach.praise: Each year's interest joins the money, so next year's interest is bigger. My savings will grow faster!
teach.nudge: What happens to the first year's interest in the second year?

topics.title: Using percentages to compare and check

learn.hook: Ravi got 45 out of 60. Sita got 38 out of 50. Who did better? Raw marks can fool you — percentages tell the truth.
points: To compare scores out of different totals, change each to a percentage: Ravi 45/60 = 75%, Sita 38/50 = 76%. Sita did slightly better.
From a ratio to percentages: boys : girls = 3 : 2 means boys are 3/5 = 60% and girls are 40%.
On ingredient labels, the parts add up to 100%: wheat 60%, sugar 25%, oil 12%, so everything else is 3%.
Check whether a claim can be true: in a class of 30, '40% are boys' means 12 boys. A claim of 35% of 30 people (10.5 people) cannot be exactly true.

example.q: Team A won 18 of 24 matches, Team B won 21 of 30. Which team has the better record?

learn.reallife: Board exam results, cricket strike rates and election results are compared using percentages.

games.title: Can it be exactly true for a class of 40?

quiz.q: Ravi scored 45 out of 60 and Sita scored 38 out of 50. Who did better?
quiz.mistake: Compares raw marks with different totals

quiz.q: Team A won 18 of 24 matches; Team B won 21 of 30. Which team has a better winning percentage?
quiz.explain: A: 75%, B: 70%. Team A is better even though it won fewer matches.
quiz.mistake: Compares the numbers of wins only

quiz.q: In a club, boys : girls = 3 : 2. What percentage of the club are boys?
quiz.explain: Boys are 3 out of every 5, and 3/5 = 60%.
quiz.mistake: Uses 3/2 or 3 out of 10

quiz.q: A drink is mixed as concentrate : water = 1 : 4. What percentage of the drink is concentrate?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 4 instead of the total 5

quiz.q: A biscuit label says wheat 60%, sugar 25%, oil 12%, and the rest is salt and flavours. What percentage is the rest?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the parts must total 100%

quiz.q: A 200 g pack of dal says protein is 12%. How many grams of protein does it contain?
quiz.mistake: Reads 12% as 12 g

quiz.q: Which claim about a class of 30 students could be exactly true?
quiz.explain: 40% of 30 = 12, so 12 boys fits. 35% of 30 = 10.5 and 25% of 30 = 7.5 are not whole numbers of students.
quiz.mistake: Does not check that a percentage of people gives a whole number

quiz.q: Two friends share sweets in the ratio 7 : 13. What percentage does the first friend get?
quiz.mistake: Takes the second share or uses 7/13

teach.ask: Gappu scored 18 out of 20, and Pari scored 40 out of 50. Pari says she won because 40 is bigger. Is she right?
teach.praise: My 18/20 is 90%, Pari's 40/50 is 80%. I did better! Percentages make it fair.
teach.nudge: Are the two tests out of the same total? How can you make them fair to compare?
